title: General Gordon's two-digit numeral note to the Mudir of Dongola, 1884 (Durham SAD.250/1/550)

steps.what: Opened leaves 549 and 550 on Durham's free IIIF server; the server caps a request at 1024 px a side, so leaf 550 (2107 x 3264) was read in tiles and row strips.
DECODE, Tomokiyo (all pages and GL.htm), Lasry and web searches, and Hake's Journals (Appendix U) for a printed or published decipherment of a Gordon note to the Mudir of Dongola.
Read the leaf row by row into 119 two-digit groups in reading order, noting struck-and-corrected cells and lighter-ink groups; the 3/4 and 2/6 glyph pairs are uncertain.
26 distinct values in 119 groups, coincidence index 0.065, first digit in 1,2,3,5,6,7,8 and second in 2,4,5,7,8,9 in 116 of 119 groups: a structured table, letters of a text repeating.

Read both Arabic-alphabet number columns (N1, N2) of Durham SAD.250/1/81 at 1.5x (27 of 28 letters, readings graded H/M/L) and mapped the note through each, as read and digit-reversed, with and without 3=4 and 2=6, scoring the letters against Arabic unigram frequencies (ar-wikipedia-sample) with a random-reassignment null (4000 draws).

Digit-grid test: 95 percent of the note's groups have first digit in 1,2,3,5,6,7,8 and second in 2,4,5,7,8,9 (52 percent for random 1-9 pairs); table N2 78 percent, N1 44 percent. N2 may be a keying of the same family; N1 is not.

Read the clear Arabic (address, 'as previously written', 'each', two closing lines about the aforementioned men not being given something and a payment to each); suggests the groups may carry names or sums, not running prose. Model reading, no human Arabic reader.

Key-free structure test against 3000 shuffles and 3000 real 119-letter Arabic slices: repeated bigrams (31) and trigrams (7) are 3.2 and 4.0 SD above shuffles and ordinary for Arabic, but the commonest bigram occurs 4 times (real Arabic about 9) and 26 distinct symbols exceed the real mean of 22.

Monoalphabetic Arabic substitution attack (letter trigram model) on the 26 symbols, with 20 shuffled-note controls and 20 held-out-Arabic controls: the note scores above every shuffle and below every real control; the decode is not Arabic. Splicing in the clear words changes nothing.

Crib dragging: the last four groups (38 75 34 49, after the clear words 'did not give them') forced to each of 156 common four-letter Arabic words and re-optimised, calibrated against 156 random cribs; 12 of 156 beat the random 95th percentile (about 8 expected) and none yields readable text.

Surveyed the digitised Durham Nile Campaign units (SAD.250/1/1-133, 528-606; 278 leaves) for other numeral leaves or the earlier letter the note cites: only leaf 550 itself; the TNA Kitchener telegrams in Arabic script (PRO 30/57/4/75-109), SAD.101/15, the Hicks registers and the 1916 Arab Bureau files are not digitised.

outcome.method_basis: Transcription, statistics, a first reading of the clear Arabic, the Durham key table (both Arabic columns as read) and a crib attack are done and none reads the note: the table fails, a letter-substitution attack scores between the shuffled and real-Arabic controls, and no crib on the closing groups stands out. The note's order is structured, so it is not noise; a code carrying names or sums is the likelier system.
outcome.fraction_read_source: transcription.txt, cipher tokens (119 groups, none given a value)
outcome.notes: Next: the physical sources (TNA PRO 30/57/4/75-109 at Kew, Durham SAD.101/15, SAD.866 and SAD.600) for the repeated units or the earlier letter; a human Arabic reader for clear_words.md.

prior.where: None found in DECODE, Tomokiyo, Lasry or Hake's edition of the Khartoum journals.

human: The project owner asked for the target folder and the test of the Durham key table SAD.250/1/81 after the lead was vetted and promoted; no target-specific intervention recorded.
